slots.practicalActivity: On paper (or in a text file), design the three-level namespace for a hypothetical company with a finance team and a marketing team: name one metastore, two catalogs (one per team), and at least two schemas inside each catalog. Write the fully-qualified three-part name (catalog.schema.table) for one table you'd expect to find in each schema.
slots.deliverable: A sketched metastore -> catalog -> schema -> table hierarchy with at least four fully-qualified three-part table names.

slots.practicalActivity: For three tables -- a brand-new table your pipeline will own end to end, a years-old data lake path you're bringing under governance without moving the files, and a registered ML model -- decide and justify managed vs. external for the two tables, then write the real CREATE TABLE statement for the external one, including its LOCATION clause pointing at a plausible cloud path.
slots.deliverable: A managed-vs-external decision with justification for two tables, plus one real CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION statement for the external table.

lessons.title: Principals: Users, Groups and Service Principals

slots.practicalActivity: Write the three GRANT statements needed for a group named bi-readers to query marketing.campaigns.leads -- the full USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT chain, not just SELECT alone. Then write the single REVOKE statement that would undo just the SELECT grant, and name who (by ownership rule) is allowed to run all four statements.
slots.deliverable: Three correct GRANT statements forming the full read chain, one REVOKE statement, and a one-sentence ownership justification.

slots.practicalActivity: A principal currently has only SELECT on finance.accounts_payable.invoices. Write the two additional GRANT statements they need before they can actually query it, explaining in one sentence why SELECT alone wasn't enough. Then write the single GRANT ON SCHEMA statement that would make every future table in that schema automatically readable by the same principal, and explain why that's an inheritance behavior worth being deliberate about.
slots.deliverable: Two completing GRANT statements with a one-sentence explanation, plus one schema-level GRANT demonstrating future-child inheritance.

slots.practicalActivity: Permissions lab: starting from nothing, write the full GRANT sequence for a new data-engineers group to have MANAGE on a catalog named ops, and for a narrower reporting-analysts group to read (and only read) one specific table three levels down inside it. Then write the ALTER TABLE OWNER TO statement transferring ownership of that table to a named service principal, and explain in one sentence what changes about who can grant further access once ownership moves.
slots.deliverable: A complete, correctly-ordered GRANT sequence for two principals with different privilege levels, plus one ownership-transfer statement with its consequence explained.

slots.practicalActivity: Using a table you can create in your own workspace (or describe hypothetically), write a row filter function that lets members of an admin group see every row and restricts everyone else to rows where department = 'engineering'. Apply it with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER, then write the ALTER TABLE ... DROP ROW FILTER statement and explain why it must run before dropping the underlying filter function.
slots.deliverable: A working row filter function, the ALTER TABLE statement applying it, and the correctly-ordered DROP ROW FILTER statement with its reasoning.

lessons.title: Attribute-Based Access Control and Governed Tags

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one sensitive column type from this course's scope (e.g. ssn, salary, email) and design a governed tag you'd apply to every column of that kind across every schema in a catalog. Write one sentence describing the ABAC policy you'd attach to that tag (who gets access, who gets masked), and name one Unity Catalog mechanism from the last two lessons that policy would actually be enforced by.
slots.deliverable: A named governed tag with its ABAC policy description and the enforcement mechanism it maps to.

slots.practicalActivity: Fine-grained security lab: for a single hypothetical table with a region column and a phone_number column, write a row filter restricting non-admins to their own region AND a column mask (via dynamic view or masking function) that partially redacts phone_number for every role except admins. Combine both on the same table and write one sentence on how the two mechanisms stack independently, the same way masking and row filtering stack in this course's Snowflake counterpart.
slots.deliverable: A combined row-filter-plus-column-mask design for one table, with a written explanation of how the two controls stack.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a table you have access to in any Databricks workspace (or describe one hypothetically) with a column named ssn. Write the system.access.column_lineage query that answers 'if I change this column's format, which downstream tables break?' Then write the three GRANT statements needed for a data-governance-team group to read system.access, following the same USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT chain the system catalog requires like any other catalog.
slots.deliverable: A working column_lineage query answering a real blast-radius question, plus the three GRANT statements opening read access to system.access.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the GRANT statements needed to let a finops group read system.billing.usage and system.billing.list_prices but nothing else in the system catalog. Then write the filtered query (using a WHERE clause on a date column, since unfiltered system-table queries fail outright) that would find the single most expensive day in the last 30 days, and name one monitoring or compliance report you'd schedule on top of it.
slots.deliverable: Scoped GRANT statements for billing-only access, a correctly-filtered cost query, and one named compliance report built on it.

slots.practicalActivity: Discovery and audit lab: combine what you've learned across lineage and system tables into one exercise. Write a system.access.column_lineage query tracing a sensitive column (e.g. ssn) to every downstream table, then write a second query against system.access.audit (or describe its real columns) that would show every user who queried that same sensitive table in the last 7 days, for a GDPR-style data-subject access request.
slots.deliverable: Two chained queries: one tracing a sensitive column's downstream lineage, one auditing who accessed the source table recently.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a Delta Sharing arrangement for sharing one table with an external business partner who has no Databricks account: name the share, the table inside it, and one governance control (an expiration date or a row filter) you'd apply before sharing. Then, for a registered ML model in Unity Catalog, name which Chapter 2/3 permission (GRANT, row filter, or tag-based ABAC) would apply to restrict who can score against it in production.
slots.deliverable: A named Delta Share design with one governance control, plus a named permission mechanism restricting access to one ML model.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a three-phase migration plan for moving a legacy, ungoverned Hive metastore's tables into Unity Catalog: which tables become external (registered in place, no data movement) versus managed, in what order, and what you'd verify (grants, lineage, ownership) before decommissioning the old metastore. Then complete the course's own practice lab exercise end to end, tracking which of its tasks you completed without looking back at earlier lessons.
slots.deliverable: A three-phase migration plan naming managed/external decisions and verification steps, plus a completed run of the course's practice lab.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a one-to-two-page Unity Catalog governance plan for a hypothetical mid-size company bringing three teams (finance, marketing, data science) onto one lakehouse. Cover the catalog/schema structure, a GRANT chain for one cross-team table, one row filter or column mask protecting a sensitive column, how you'd use lineage and system tables to audit access after the fact, and one Delta Sharing or migration decision.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written Unity Catalog governance plan covering namespace design, a permission chain, one fine-grained control, an audit approach, and one lakehouse-governance decision.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a Unity Catalog namespace, write the real GRANT/REVOKE chains that govern read and write access, attach row filters and column masks to protect sensitive data, trace lineage and query system tables to prove access controls worked, and plan a governed migration or Delta Sharing arrangement -- the full hands-on Unity Catalog governance skillset the Data Governance Engineer path assumes a student can execute, not just describe.
